spots.name: Cape Spartel
spots.label: Cape Spartel

text.directions_text: There are no Underground, rail or tram stops nearby, so reach the area by road via the National Road S701 from Tangier. The lighthouse is roughly 12 to 14 km from the city. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.geographic_location: Cape Spartel is on the Atlantic coast about 12 km west of Tangier, at the north-western tip of Morocco where the Strait of Gibraltar begins.
text.access_note: The grounds are a visitor site, and access to the tower and museum may need a ticket or have restrictions, so check the official site before you go.
text.description: Cape Spartel is the headland where Morocco's Atlantic coast meets the Strait of Gibraltar. It stands about 300 metres above the sea, some 12 km west of Tangier, and is the north-westernmost point of the African continent. The red-and-white lighthouse, built under Sultan Muhammad IV in 1864, sits at the end of a cliff. It is a good subject for a phone because the tower is simple and bold. The place is also known as the point where the Mediterranean and the Atlantic are said to meet, and Spain can be seen across the strait on a clear day. The whole site was renovated in 2020-2021 and now has a maritime museum, a restaurant and a botanical garden, so there is plenty to see before or after your photos. Keep a few paces back from any cliff edge, because it is windy and the rocks can be slippery. Hold the phone with both hands, and take a few frames of each view in case the wind makes you wobble.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Otherwise use the default lens (1x) and accept that the tower will be small in the frame, which can work well for a sense of scale. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the wider headland and a lot of sky, or for the signpost.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day, and check on your screen where the sun sits before you shoot, so that it is not shining straight into your lens as you look towards the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here, look north-east to find the red-and-white tower on the headland. Keep well back from any cliff edge while you take your shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the tower on one of the vertical lines, with the horizon on a horizontal line so the sea stays level. Leave some empty space beside the tower to give a sense of the distance. As an alternative, find the Cap Spartel sign, which shows the Atlantic on one side and the Mediterranean on the other. On a clear day Spain may show in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white parts and the sky keep their detail. Take a few shots in a row because of the wind, and keep your elbows tucked in to stay steady.

spots.name: Kasbah Palace, Tangier
spots.label: Kasbah Palace

text.directions_text: There are no Underground, rail or tram stops to give you here, so head for the Kasbah at the top of Tangier's old town and ask for Bab el Assa or Place de la Kasbah. Walk the last stretch on foot, as the lanes are narrow and step downhill. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.geographic_location: In the Kasbah, the old citadel at the top of Tangier's medina, on high ground looking over the old town roofs and the Strait of Gibraltar. The palace is in the eastern part of the Kasbah, and Bab el Assa is a gate and lane just beside it.
text.access_note: The lane and the outside views are open public streets, but the Kasbah Museum inside the palace is a separate matter, so check on site before you go if you want to go in.
text.description:
The Kasbah Palace, also called Dar el Makhzen, is the old governor's residence at the top of Tangier's citadel. It was built in the early 18th century under Sultan Moulay Ismail, on the ruins of an English castle. It has been a museum since 1922, and it reopened after a big renovation in 2016. Inside, two courtyards have decorated wooden ceilings and marble fountains. From outside, what you notice is the whitewashed walls on one of the highest points of the old town, looking over the medina roofs and the Strait of Gibraltar.

From here the photo is not of the palace itself. You get an arched gateway and a white lane framing a slice of blue sea. One guide calls it the classic Kasbah photo, and it works well on a phone because the narrow walls lead the eye straight to the water. The palace stands a very short walk to the north-west, so treat this as a good extra shot beside the palace views.

For the palace itself, Place de la Kasbah shows its white walls and sloping battlements with the port, rooftops and the strait beyond. Dar el Makhzen's own exterior has the walls in the foreground with the bay below. Take the outside views first, and check on site before you go if you want to go inside.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole gateway, the white walls and the sea in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a detail such as the arch or a patch of sea.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late in the day, when the light turns warm, according to one guide.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Bab el Assa (lane beside the gate, stepping down toward the strait). An arched gateway and white lane framing a slice of blue sea; the palace itself is not in the frame. In the lane beside the gate where it steps down towards the strait. From here you see the arched gateway and the white lane framing a slice of blue sea. The palace is not in the frame; it is just to the north-west, so walk that way for pictures of the palace walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the arch or lane edges on the outer lines so the walls lead the eye to the sea. Keep the phone level so the walls do not lean. Then walk to Place de la Kasbah or Dar el Makhzen for the palace's white walls with the port and bay behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bright sea or sky to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white walls keep their detail rather than turning pale and flat. A Live Photo can catch someone walking through the gateway.

spots.name: Kasbah Mosque, Tangier
spots.label: Kasbah Mosque

text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops near here, so head for the kasbah in the old city of Tangier. Once you are in the kasbah, look for Rue Ibn Abbou, the lane beside the entrance to the palace and museum. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.geographic_location: In the kasbah, the old royal citadel in the medina of Tangier. The mosque stands directly south of the kasbah palace, which is now a museum.
text.access_note: Rue Ibn Abbou is an open public lane, but the mosque is a place of worship, so dress modestly and respect worshippers, and check locally before going inside.
text.description:
The Kasbah Mosque is the main Friday mosque of Tangier's old royal citadel, and it dates from the late 17th century. It was built after the English left the city in 1684, when Sultan Moulay Ismail had the kasbah rebuilt as a walled district for the governor and his government. The minaret and the decorated entrance were added later by the grandson of the governor who built the mosque.

The outside is the part to photograph. The entrance is a Moorish arch with radiating geometric patterns, and the gaps are filled with colourful zellij tilework. Above it rises a minaret with an octagonal shaft, which is unusual in Morocco, where most are square. Its faces carry blind arches, more tilework and panels of sebka patterns.

The mosque is tucked into narrow lanes, so you can't back away for a wide view. The best free street-level angle is from Rue Ibn Abbou, in front of the main entrance, next to the entrance of the Dar el-Makhzen palace. From there you see the arched doorway with the minaret above the lane. Stand centred for a tidy, symmetrical shot, then move in for the tile details. If you want the wider setting afterwards, Place de la Kasbah has a broad view over the city, the harbour and the Strait. Check the view on arrival, as the mosque may not be easy to see from there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the narrow lane, so the arch, the doorway and the minaret all fit. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look at the entrance. A telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is good for the tilework and the top of the minaret.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Pick a quieter moment, as the lane is narrow and people pass through. Check the light when you arrive, because the lane may be shaded.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Rue Ibn Abbou (in front of the mosque's main entrance, next to the Dar el-Makhzen palace entrance). The arched entrance to the mosque, with the minaret visible above the lane. Walk north-east to Rue Ibn Abbou and stand in front of the mosque's main entrance, next to the entrance of the Dar el-Makhzen palace. From there the arched doorway and the minaret rising above the lane come into view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the doorway up with the centre of the frame, keeping the minaret upright above it. Hold the phone level and tilt it up only slightly, so the walls don't lean too much. For a second picture, move closer and zoom in on the zellij and sebka patterns. Place de la Kasbah is a good alternative if you want a wide view of the city and the Strait.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the doorway to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky doesn't wash out the tilework. Lanes like this are often half in shade.
